segments.title: Setting up and discussing his father's Conn Victor cornet
segments.summary: Hirsch shows the interviewer his father's Conn Victor-model horn and its tuning shanks; talk of Tony Fusero and cleaning it.

segments.title: Reel start: name, date and phone number for the tape
segments.summary: Hirsch gives his full name, spelling, the date 27 October 1987 and his phone number for the record.

segments.title: What burlesque opera is; a light opera at the Civic Theater
segments.summary: Hirsch tries to recall the name of a show he played at the Civic Theater, a light opera with a couple of hit songs, before a phone call interrupts.

segments.title: His father's work running the family business
segments.summary: After his grandfather died his father ran his grandmother's business, bought it from the estate and incorporated it about 1915; Hirsch later inherited it.

segments.title: His father's spot jobs and the musicians' union building on Bourbon Street
segments.summary: His father played trumpet taps at Italian society events, was vice president of Local 174 and engineered the cheap Depression purchase of the union home; a larger Elks building was turned down.

segments.title: His father as a soloist and in the Shriners Band; the Junior Shrine Band
segments.summary: Hirsch describes his father as a soloist and assistant leader of the Shriners Band, its fine players, his own drum study and the Junior Shrine Band trip to Washington in 1923; mention of Wade Schlegel.

segments.title: Raymond Scott, Lou Shuby, Johnny Williams and New York studio players
segments.summary: Talk of Wade Schlegel's brother with Raymond Scott in California, bassist Lou Shuby, drummer Johnny Williams, and Hirsch's own work with Studebaker transcriptions and sitting in at NBC while in the Navy.

segments.title: Phil Harris's compliment when Hirsch planned to leave
segments.summary: Phil Harris told his band that Hirsch was like a fly in a zipper, meaning the band was no good without him.

segments.chapter: Growing up: theaters and the lakefront
segments.title: Spanish Fort concert band and teacher Armin Vesey
segments.summary: As a child of ten or twelve Hirsch went with his father to hear the concert band at Spanish Fort and talks about Armin Vesey and his trumpet teaching.

segments.chapter: Growing up: theaters and the lakefront
segments.title: Liberty Theater usher job, the Sanger Theater drum job and Lou Forbes
segments.summary: Hirsch worked as an usher at the Liberty, learned its theater musicians, then took over the drum chair at the Sanger when Gosley quit and learned stage presence from Lou Forbes.

segments.chapter: Growing up: theaters and the lakefront
segments.title: Learning theater music by heart; Augie Shelang; hotel ballrooms
segments.summary: Hirsch explains that hearing the Liberty's music daily let him play it at the Sanger without reading well; he also recalls Augie Shelang and dance rooms at the Jung and Roosevelt hotels.

segments.title: Bucktown camps and the lake steamboats
segments.summary: Bucktown was summer camps with weekend dances; steamers like the Susquehanna and Mandeville ran to Mandeville with mostly black bands, and a wooden leg of Bob Aguilera turned up in the union attic.

segments.title: Union home plaque and Jacques Pepitone's WWL speech
segments.summary: Hirsch recalls the union home and a missing plaque, then tells of union president Pepitone's gaffe at the WWL 50,000-watt dedication.

segments.title: Spanish Fort by streetcar; the Southern Syncopators' Gulf Coast hotel jobs
segments.summary: Hirsch recalls riding the train to Spanish Fort as a boy and then his Southern Syncopators five-piece band at the Tivoli Hotel and Wayside Inn, with pay and room and board.

segments.title: Travelling to Biloxi: ferries, gravel roads and bad tires
segments.summary: Getting between New Orleans and Biloxi took fourteen hours or more, with ferries over the Pearl River, Honey Island swamp gravel roads and hard tires.

segments.title: Music in Biloxi: Johnny Tobin's band and the beach hotels
segments.summary: Hirsch tells what bands and dances there were in Biloxi, Gulfport and Mobile, with Johnny Tobin's band at the White House hotel, and Easter holidays at Bay St. Louis.

segments.title: The Southern Syncopators and Biloxi hotels, Mrs. Brown
segments.summary: Hirsch describes the Southern Syncopators' hotel job, Biloxi's later overbuilding and Mrs. Brown's hotel where he got a free room.

segments.title: Southern Syncopators members; Sidney Spies and Dutch Flick
segments.summary: Members of the five-piece band (Ferriot, Jelpe, Spies, Dutch Flick), the Music Box dance hall and Flick's later life.

segments.title: Buying and furnishing his Bienville property, an antique armoire
segments.summary: A digression about Roland Flick finding him his property and about taking apart the antique armoire.

segments.title: Slim Lamar and Ray Bonitas becoming a bass player
segments.summary: Hirsch recalls the band that went to Jackson, Mississippi with a Conn sales manager, where he moved from piano to drums and Ray Bonitas was made a bass player.

segments.title: The Conn band selling school bands in Mississippi; Charlie Wagner
segments.summary: Charlie Wagner and the group played school concerts to sign up students for rented instruments, which started Mississippi high-school bands, and musicians later became teachers.

segments.title: Charlie Wagner stories and losing old friends
segments.summary: Wagner's Jean Lafitte Rose publicity stunt, his Lafitte job with no union, and Hirsch's sadness at losing Ray Bonitas and other friends.

segments.title: Dance halls around Elysian Fields and the Hollywood
segments.summary: Third Ward dance halls, the open-air Hollywood owned by Sharkey and Leon Prima, Dave Winstein and Nina Pecone, and Al Rose's book.

segments.title: Playing drums with Earl Crumb's Owls Orchestra; Sieg Christensen
segments.summary: Hirsch subbed for Earl Crum in the Owls, names the members, recalls Sieg Christensen and his father, and the Owls' string-band origins.

segments.title: Dick Mackey, Wade Schlegel and Fred Waring
segments.summary: Discussion of Dick Mackey's later bands, helping Wade Schlegel (Dave Wade) start out, Wade's career with Waring and a gig story.

segments.title: Sterling Bose, Pollock and a road trip with Earl Crum
segments.summary: Hirsch recalls Sterling Bose, a trip north with Earl Crum and his wife where they saw Pollock in Detroit, and the 1933 World's Fair.

segments.title: Earl Crum's band at Suburban Gardens and Joe Cherniowski
segments.summary: Crum led the band at Suburban Gardens with Hirsch on drums and piano; Cherniowski, Paramount Publix leader, was also involved.

segments.title: Suburban Gardens personnel and Charlie Margulis's visit for the Edsel
segments.summary: Band members, Charlie Margulis's high-note playing and his advice about trumpet longevity, and his visit in 1957 for Ford's Edsel launch.

segments.title: The Tulaneans and the lost banjo on the train to Mobile
segments.summary: Hirsch recalls the Tulaneans jazz band at the Strand, then his work with Leslie George at the Battle House in Mobile when he left Leslie's guitar and banjo on the train.

segments.title: Leslie George's society orchestra
segments.summary: Leslie George led a society band using stock arrangements, no faking.

segments.title: Intermission acts at Suburban Gardens
segments.summary: Singer Carmen Di Giovanni as MC and various dance acts at Suburban Gardens.

segments.title: Louis Armstrong's broadcasts and Phil Harris in New Orleans
segments.summary: Hirsch recalls Armstrong's 1931 stint with a small band doing broadcasts and talking through the show, compared with Phil Harris at the Blue Room.

segments.title: The size and layout of Suburban Gardens, a gambling house
segments.summary: Suburban Gardens was a gambling house with a porch around the room and no air conditioning; he compares it with the Roosevelt ballroom and Beverly Club.

segments.title: New Orleans summer breezes and air conditioning
segments.summary: A digression on breezes in New Orleans and in his house and how trees and building changed it.

segments.title: Snoozer Quinn, the progressive guitarist
segments.summary: Snoozer Quinn strolled tables at Suburban Gardens, later joined Whiteman, drank, was a soloist rather than a band player, and Wiggs recorded him dying.

segments.title: The Jung Hotel band with Johnny Wiggs: stock orchestrations
segments.summary: Hirsch gives a frank opinion of the Jung Hotel band, Wiggs as a player and the personnel (Stratikas, Wolf, Fridge, Roniga, Laocana).

segments.title: The Halfway House orchestra and Merritt Brunies
segments.summary: He was too young and lived too far uptown to go to the Halfway House or the Bourbon Street dives.

segments.title: Tulane studies, Two Bits clubs and the 1932 Rose Bowl trip
segments.summary: Hirsch left Tulane architecture to play music, played Two Bits clubs and Honeysuckle Inn, had a drum shop and timpani, and went to the Rose Bowl with the Tulane band.

segments.title: Writing the Sugar Bowl Parade with Pete Fountain
segments.summary: Hirsch shows the memo sheet and press on the Sugar Bowl Parade, which he wrote with Pete Fountain and lyricist Dick Brown, adopted as the official Sugar Bowl song in 1963.

segments.title: Royalties from his compositions
segments.summary: Statements for the Sugar Bowl Parade and other pieces; Two Beat Music is now MCA.

segments.title: Funeral band for Tulane Stadium and the Pops concert
segments.summary: Hirsch looks at programs for the stadium demolition and a Pops concert where he was a soloist.

segments.title: Charles Anthony's name change and the Sugar Bowl book for the archives
segments.summary: Name changes (Charles Anthony, Wiggs), and the Sugar Bowl history book that will go to the archives.

segments.chapter: California, New York and Richard Himber
segments.title: First trip to California with Louis Prima, 1937
segments.summary: Hirsch went to California with Prima in July 1937, hoping to earn a union membership for studio work, but they left in December.

segments.chapter: California, New York and Richard Himber
segments.title: Recording and films with Prima, the Famous Door and meeting Himber
segments.summary: The Prima band personnel, the film Start Cheering, the Famous Door in New York and how Richard Himber came to hear Hirsch there.

segments.chapter: California, New York and Richard Himber
segments.title: Himber's audition and the union fixer Jack Rosenberg
segments.summary: Himber auditioned Hirsch on vibes, Local 802's president Rosenberg arranged the union side, and he played radio opens and dinner sets.

segments.chapter: California, New York and Richard Himber
segments.title: Almost joining Paul Whiteman's band
segments.summary: Hirsch wanted Whiteman's drum chair but Whiteman would not take him from his friend Himber, and George Wettling got it.

segments.chapter: California, New York and Richard Himber
segments.title: Recording with Richard Himber
segments.summary: Hirsch discusses xylophone parts and an album crediting him with Himber.

segments.chapter: California, New York and Richard Himber
segments.title: Himber's rhythmic pyramids and band-leader masks
segments.summary: Himber's band changed styles, used masks to imitate leaders' themes on radio, causing mixups at the network.

segments.title: Photo book of old bands: Owls and the Hollywood Club
segments.summary: Hirsch identifies players in old band photographs in the Rose and Souchon book.

segments.title: Camp map, Spanish Fort and lake steamboat photos
segments.summary: He points out camps, parks and the steamers Mandeville and Susquehanna, with their divided bandstands.

segments.title: Honorarium and goodbyes
segments.summary: Interviewer writes a check as honorarium and union dues; the interview ends.
